name: Ceramide NS

lead: Ceramide NS is one class of ceramide, a waxy lipid that is a major part of the skin's outer barrier. Moisturizers add ceramides to support that barrier and reduce water loss.
The appearance payoff is skin that is better hydrated, so it looks smoother and less rough or flaky.

paras: It is applied in leave-on moisturizers, creams and lotions, often alongside cholesterol and fatty acids, which together mimic the skin's natural lipid mix. People use them daily, especially for dry skin.
Topical ceramide moisturizers are generally well tolerated; a Cosmetic Ingredient Review safety assessment is cited for cosmetic use. Individual products can still irritate sensitive skin.

chain: Barrier lipid supports the skin's outer layer
angle.text: Ceramide-containing moisturizers are used to keep the barrier intact so skin looks more hydrated and even.

lead: Ceramides are waxy lipids made of sphingosine and a fatty acid. In the stratum corneum, ceramides make up about half of the lipid matrix by weight with cholesterol and free fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss [1]. NS ceramides (non-hydroxy fatty acid with sphingosine) are one of the epidermal classes [1].

Because dry or damaged barrier skin looks rough and dull, moisturizers add ceramides to support hydration. A randomised split-body trial of two over-the-counter moisturizers in adults with eczema-prone skin measured hydration, water loss and skin ceramide NS and AS levels over 4 weeks [2]. Researchers have also modelled ceramide NS in simulations of the skin lipid matrix [3][4] and engineered yeast to produce human ceramide NS because supply from animal or plant sources is limited [5].

paras: The stratum corneum is described as bricks (corneocytes) and mortar (lipids); ceramides about 50%, cholesterol about 25%, free fatty acids about 15% [1]. Ceramide levels can fall with dry air, harsh sulfates, UV exposure and aging [1]. Dry skin research has catalogued molecular markers of xerosis [6].
Ceramides appear in soaps, shampoos, creams and sunscreens, and in some eczema-supporting topicals [1].
Metabolically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae produced human ceramide NS in a 2015 study, aimed at the limited supply from animal or plant sources [5].

In a randomised, double-blind split-body study, moisturizers applied twice daily for 4 weeks to adults with eczema-prone skin were assessed with corneometer hydration, transepidermal water loss and tape-stripped ceramide NS and AS levels [2]. Other work on ceramide NS is computational or in animal and lab settings, including molecular dynamics simulations [3][4].
